# What changes now {#sec-ch22}

::: {.epigraph by="William Gibson, attributed"}
The future is already here. It's just not very evenly distributed.
:::

You've come a long way: probability and calibration, neural networks, attention, LLMs and agents, then a new kind of model and everything it takes to use one well. This short last chapter steps back and asks what it all means, for the industry and for you.

Most predictions about AI soon look foolish, so I'll keep to three things: what the book showed, what it suggests, and what nobody knows yet.

::: {.goals}
- See the decision layer as its own layer in an AI system, separate from generation.
- Estimate what moving decisions out of an LLM changes for one of your own tasks.
- Know which skills become more valuable when decisions get cheap.
- Keep a clear list of what isn't known yet.
- Leave with a plan for your first three months.
:::

## A layer of its own

For the last few years, the default AI system has been one big model doing everything (reading, deciding, writing, calling tools), all as text.

![Two ways to build an AI system. Left: one model does everything as text. Right: each layer does one job. An LLM reads and writes, a decision layer answers typed questions with probabilities, a policy turns those into actions, and tools, logs and people sit underneath.](/figures/ch29/stack.pdf){#fig-stack}

The right side of @fig-stack is the design this book kept arriving at. The LLM does what only an LLM can: read anything, write for people. The decision layer answers small typed questions in one pass, with probabilities you can test. The policy sets thresholds from costs and capacity. Underneath, tools act and people review.

Each layer is smaller than the system, testable on its own with Part I's tools, and replaceable without rebuilding the rest. That, more than any benchmark, is why I think this split will last.

::: {.keyidea}
Split the system: the LLM reads and writes, the decision layer decides, the policy acts, people own the costs.
:::

## What gets cheap

Take one agent task: a ticket arrives; the agent picks tools, checks whether it has enough, checks whether an action is safe, does it, and writes a reply.

![One illustrative agent task, with its decisions made by an LLM or by a decision model. The writing step costs the same either way; the decisions are where the difference is.](/figures/ch29/task.pdf){#fig-task}

With the book's illustrative LLM figures and Jev's vendor-reported ones, the task drops from about {{< num ch29 task_llm_s int >}} seconds to {{< num ch29 task_jev_s int >}}. The cost falls by about three quarters (@fig-task). What's left is mostly the one step where an LLM writes for a person. (Chapter 17's hybrid agent ran about {{< num ch29 ch24_speedup int >}} times faster for the same reason.)

Then Chapter 12's warning applies. We won't make the same decisions for less; we'll make many more: every login checked, every retrieved passage judged, every agent step gated. The big change won't come from doing today's work more cheaply. It'll come from work that becomes worth doing.

## What gets valuable

If deciding gets cheap, what becomes scarce?

Judgement about the decision itself. Someone still has to decide what a mistake costs, where the thresholds go, how much the review queue can take, and whether the probabilities are still calibrated this week. No model does that for you.

::: {.keyidea}
When deciding gets cheap, judgement about the decision itself becomes scarce.
:::

![Skills that matter more when decisions get cheap, and skills that matter less on their own, with the chapters that teach each.](/figures/ch29/skills.pdf){#fig-skills}

That's why Part I was worth the long way round. Thinking in probabilities and testing calibration are the foundations (@fig-skills): the difference between a system that makes a million cheap decisions well and one that makes a million cheap mistakes. What matters less *on its own* is prompt-writing for everything and picking the biggest model by default. Both are still useful; neither is the whole job any more.

## What nobody knows yet

@fig-unknowns is the book's "unknown" pile, as it stands today.

![Open questions, and what you can do about each today.](/figures/ch29/unknowns.pdf){#fig-unknowns}

Every item is still open; none is a reason to wait. Calibration on your data is a test you can run this week. Version changes are handled by a pinned version and a monitor. Prices are a spreadsheet. And the pattern will outlast any one vendor: a typed question in, a probability out, and a policy in your own code can move to a different model in an afternoon. You don't need to predict how this turns out.

::: {.keyidea}
You need decisions you can measure, thresholds you can move and a model you can replace.
:::

## What to do on Monday

![A first three months, one decision at a time.](/figures/ch29/monday.pdf){#fig-monday}

If you do one thing after closing this book, do the audit in the first box of @fig-monday: list every decision your system makes, and count them. Most people are surprised how many there are, and how many are small, typed and frequent.

Then pick *one*. Get a few hundred labels. Test its calibration. Put prices on its mistakes, set its thresholds, run it in shadow mode. Switch it on with a fail-safe and a monitor. Then do the next one. It isn't exciting. It's how every system in this book got better.

::: {.breaks}
This chapter is the least certain in the book. The cost and speed figures are illustrative, and Jev's are vendor-reported from its early access. The claim that a decision layer will become a standard part of AI systems is my reading of the evidence here, not a finding. It could be wrong if general models become fast enough and well calibrated enough that splitting stops being worth it. If that happens, the skills in @fig-skills still apply; only the box they sit in changes.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Your own system: pick the decision in it that happens most often. What does a wrong "yes" cost? A wrong "no"? Where does the threshold go? And how would you know, a month from now, whether the probabilities behind it are still calibrated?

(There's no answer at the back of the book for this one. If you can fill in all four, you've learned what this book set out to teach.)
:::

Alan Turing ended his most famous paper with a sentence that fits this moment: "We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done" [@turing1950].

## The story, one more time

![The whole book as one story.](/figures/ch29/journey.pdf){#fig-journey}

@fig-journey is the book in six lines. You know where everything on that map is now. What's left is choosing the first decision in your own work that deserves this care.

::: {.exercises}
1. Write the decision audit for one system you know: every decision, how often it happens, what a mistake costs, and who owns it.
2. Write a one-page note to your team proposing the first decision to move. Use the book's words: costs, thresholds, calibration, shadow mode, fail-safe.
:::
